Public Comment: The public is encouraged to address City Council on any matter listed on the agenda or on any other matter
within its jurisdiction subject to the rules of decorum described in Section 2.08.020 of the Norwalk Municipal Code. If you wish to
address City Council, please complete a speaker card and hand the card to the Sergeant at Arms. City Council will hear public
comment on items listed on the agenda during discussion of the matter and prior to a vote and on matters not listed on the
agenda during the Oral Communications period.

Pursuant to provisions of the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the agenda, or unless certain
emergency or special circumstances exist. The City Council may direct staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for
consideration at a future City Council meeting.

Please adhere to the following procedures when addressing the City Council: Comments should be limited to 3 minutes or less.
Comments should be directed to the City Council as a whole and not directed to individual Councilmembers.

Americans with Disabilities Act: In compliance with the ADA, if you need special assistance to participate in a City meeting or
other services offered by this City, please contact the City Clerk’s department, (562) 929-5720. Assisted listening devices are
available at this meeting. Ask the City Clerk if you desire to use this device. Upon request, the agenda and documents in the
agenda packet can be made available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability. Notification of at least 48
hours prior to the meeting or time when services are needed will assist the City staff in assuring that reasonable arrangements
can be made to provide accessibility to the meeting or service.

Note: Any writings and/or documents provided to a majority of the City Council regarding any item on this agenda after it has
been posted will also be made available for public inspection. Writings and/or documents are available for inspection in the City
Clerk’s Department, during regular business hours, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., Monday – Thursday and 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., every
other Friday; telephone (562) 929-5720. You may also contact the City Clerk via e-mail at recordsrequests@norwalkca.gov.

amount contributed and the name(s) of the contributor(s). "G.C. § 84308: Yes" on this agenda indicates that the item is subject to

  REGULAR MEETING

Mayor Ayala called the meeting to order at 6:50 p.m. in the Council Chambers, Norwalk
City Hall, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard, Norwalk, California. Responding to roll call were
Councilmember Rios, Vice Mayor Perez, and Mayor Ayala. Councilmembers Ramirez
and Valencia were absent. Also present were Jesus M. Gomez, City Manager; Arnold M.
Alvarez, City Attorney; and Camille Moreno, Assistant City Clerk.

The invocation was delivered by Pastor Arthur McKibben, Norwalk Church of the
Nazarene; followed by the flag salute, led by Young Marine Private First Class Laureano
Jimenez.

CLOSED SESSION REPORT

in closed session.

Mayor Ayala approved members of the Adaptive Recreation Program to address City Council.

and Alfredo Garcia-S.

CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS

Councilmember Rios reported on her meeting with the Mexican Consulate General and
provided the phone number to a 24/7 immigration information hotline; thanked Housing
Manager Bethani Cardenas and her staff for the Foster Youth Voucher Program; and
requested the meeting be adjourned in memory of Frances Mary Husack. Vice Mayor
Perez mentioned the upcoming heat warning and shared the City will have cooling
centers available; thanked the Communications and Public Affairs team for sharing
information on new legislation; reported on her attendance at the League of California
Cities – Los Angeles Division Meeting, the Front Street Friday Night event, and the
California Joint Powers Insurance Authority Panel in Oxnard where she participated as a
panelist and spoke to newly elected officials. Mayor Ayala thanked Finance, Public
Services, Public Safety, Social Services, and Recreation staff for all the successful
summer events.

CITY MANAGER COMMENTS

Mr. Gomez shared information on heat advisory cooling stations; provided an update on
the upcoming Metropolitan Reconnecting Neighborhood and Communities Meeting; and
announced Seniors will be recognized in the month of September.

Background:

The Public Services Department (Public Services) is responsible for the management,
operations and maintenance (O&M) of the City’s water, sewer, and storm drain systems; street
lights, traffic signals traffic signage and pavement striping/markings. In addition, Public Services
also implements the City’s capital improvement program (CIP), which includes: roadways, traffic
signals, underground utilities (water, sewer and storm drains), facilities (city and park) and
associated projects. Included with the capital program are the necessary system master plans
(water, sewer, storm drain); pavement management plan, facilities and other essential
studies. These studies help staff evaluate needs and prioritize improvement projects.

Public Services is currently engaged with water main replacement projects, well rehabilitation
projects, water treatment implementation projects, Supervisory Data and Acquisition (SCADA)
system implementation, smart water meter projects, storm drain planning and catch basin
modifications projects, sewer and manhole repair and replacement projects, and grant
management.

Recently, Public Services has been experiencing increased demand for development activity
reviews. Input from Public Services helps ensure proposed developments and their
recommended improvements are compliant with applicable codes and compatible with
current/future service delivery. This increased demand is in addition to the O&M and CIP
workload from both current and planned future projects. At the current staffing levels, the
quantity and quality of work is not sustainable. Additional contract services and resources are
required to supplement project management, design, construction support, and O&M. Contract

Background:

funds to replace the backhoe loader for the Street Maintenance Division. The current unit was
placed into service in 2013 and has reached the end of its service life. Furthermore, the unit
experiences frequent breakdowns and part replacements are difficult to find.

utilized for carrying / transporting materials, street right-of-way clean-ups (i.e. emergency
services to pick up streetlight knockdowns, remove fallen trees, clearing of debris.), road repairs,
and various other departmental and interdepartmental projects (i.e. moving concrete picnic
tables within City parks). Public Services staff in all sections are cross-trained to utilize the
backhoe loader for these multiple purposes.

Staff have become aware of a cooperative purchasing agreement for construction equipment
with Case Construction allowing the City to purchase the unit locally through Sonsray Machinery
of Santa Fe Springs, California for a significant cost savings.

SUBJECT: ORDINANCE OF THE CITY OF NORWALK AMENDING NORWALK
  MUNICIPAL CODE CHAPTERS 8.48 AND 8.5 RELATING TO SOLID WASTE
  HANDLING AND RECYCLING AND ORGANIC WASTE DISPOSAL
  REDUCTION

Background:

The City of Norwalk currently relies on a two-stream waste collection system in which businesses
separate organics into one bin while placing all other materials, trash and recyclables, into a
single mixed-waste bin. This mixed waste is transported to Material Recovery Facilities (MRFs),
where recyclables are extracted from the trash stream through a combination of mechanical
sorting equipment and manual labor. The remaining non-recyclable material is then disposed of
in a landfill.

In the past, this process helped the City meet the State’s ‘high diversion’ requirements, but as
of January 1, 2025, CalRecycle has raised the minimum recovery rate for High Diversion Organic
Waste Processing Facilities from 50% to 75%. Meeting this higher threshold would require
significant capital investments and lead to material increased rates for commercial customers.
As an alternative option used in a number of jurisdictions in California, Athens Services
recommends transitioning to a three-container collection system, which offers a more cost-
effective and sustainable path to compliance. The facilities used by Athens Services do not
qualify under the new standards, and as a result, the City may be considered out of compliance
with State mandates if they do not move into a three-stream collection system.

To address this regulatory shift, staff recommends updating Chapter 8.5 of the Norwalk
Municipal Code (NMC) to transition commercial accounts to a three-stream collection system.
While organics are already collected separately, this update will also require recyclables to be
separated at the source, alongside solid waste. This approach reduces reliance on MRF

performance by ensuring that cleaner, less contaminated materials enter recycling and
composting facilities directly. In addition to ensuring regulatory compliance, source separation
improves the quality and marketability of recovered materials, reduces contamination fees, and
can lower long-term disposal costs. Amending the NMC now allows the City to establish the
necessary framework, ensuring a smooth and enforceable transition before State deadlines take
effect.

Cost to Businesses

Businesses may experience adjustments in service costs over the next few years as the new
three-stream collection system is implemented. City staff, in coordination with the City’s franchise
waste hauler, Athens Services, will work proactively to support businesses in meeting the new
requirements. The focus will be on providing education, outreach, and technical assistance to
achieve compliance well before the State mandates stricter enforcement measures, including
the potential assessment of monetary penalties for non-compliance.

SUBJECT:  HERMOSILLO PARK REHABILITATION, STORMWATER CAPTURE AND
  INFILTRATION PROJECT UPDATE

Background:

The Hermosillo Park Master Plan project began with a vision to revitalize the park, making it serve
as a community hub for the southeast portion of the city. The top priorities for a redesigned
Hermosillo Park were to construct a new state-of-the-art community center with a banquet hall
capacity of 200 people. The community center will also serve as the center piece of an overall
Hermosillo Park revitalization project that replaces and upgrade park amenities. In response to
community input, two new soccer fields with a lighting system will be installed to provide recreation
opportunities currently not available at other Norwalk parks.

Along with the City’s goals to provide active living opportunities, the City is also promoting
sustainable environmental practices such as choosing green infrastructure and environmentally
sensitive building methods. The Hermosillo Park Rehabilitation demonstrates this commitment to
the environment with the building of the Stormwater Capture and Infiltration Project under the
proposed soccer fields. This system diverts and captures storm water to infiltrate into the ground
water to replenish the area’s vital ground water resources rather than flowing out to the Pacific
Ocean.

The Hermosillo Park Rehabilitation, Stormwater Capture and Infiltration Project will construct
11.8-acre-foot capacity sub-surface infiltration gallery with water reclaim abilities. Upon
completion, the project will provide numerous community benefits and will serve to improve water
quality in Coyote Creek and the San Gabriel River. Following concerted efforts by City leaders
and City staff, the City applied and received approval for $20.1 million of Measure W funding for
the Stormwater Capture and Infiltration Project in 2019.

The project encountered several technical and regulatory challenges during the design phase,
and the completion of the design was delayed primarily due to the higher project cost compared
to the original 2019 cost estimate. As part of the ongoing park project, staff carefully reviewed the
scope of recreational amenities in comparison to the available budget. During this process,
unforeseen expenses associated with site preparation, infrastructure requirements, and increased
construction material costs arose, resulting in a substantial increase of $20 million in the overall
project cost.

The City received an additional $9,900,000 from Measure W funds from the Watershed Area
Steering Committee (WASC), which includes funding for the soccer fields, as Measure W allows
for recreational amenities to be charged to the grant if they are incorporated into any water
infiltration projects. The funding is now being brought for routine approval at the Los Angeles
County Board of Supervisors meeting scheduled for November 2025. Including the additional
Measure W funding, the project budget is still deficit of approximately $10 million.

Due to economic forces outside the control of the City, the project’s budget is not sufficient to
include all the initially proposed recreational amenities. After evaluating options, staff prioritized
essential safety and infrastructure elements to ensure the park remains functional, accessible,
and welcoming to the community. As a result, certain recreational features such as the Splash
Pad, Basketball Court, and Handball Courts are deferred to future park upgrade projects.

While these adjustments were necessary to keep the project within the approved budget, staff
remain committed to identifying potential grant funding, sponsorship opportunities, or future
budget allocations that may allow for the phased addition of these amenities at a later time. We
recognize the importance of these recreational features to our community and will continue to
explore opportunities to enhance the park as funding resources become available.
